main.text: [III, 125] [col. 357] Chapter I.
It is proved that אפעה ephe is the viper.

Among the species of serpents, either truly or by repute, are: 1. אפעה ephe. 2. כפיר chephir. 3. עכשוב acsoub. 4. פתן pethen. 5. צבע tseboa. 6. צמאון tsimmaon. 7. צפע tsepha, or צפעני tsiphoni. 8. קפוז kippoz. 9. שחל sachal. 10. שפיפון sephiphon. 11. שרף saraph. 12. תנין thannin, which is also לויתן leviathan. The matter therefore requires that we speak of each one and try to distinguish these species from one another, although this is a very difficult thing, since in Scripture hardly anything is said of one species that is not common to all. Nor are the translators consistent. Still, I shall say what seems closest to the truth. In this chapter we shall deal with אפעה ephe, which is first in alphabetical order.

In the History of the Second Temple, p. 135, it is said of Cleopatra: וקראה להביאו [col. 358] לה אפעה והכנסתו תחת דדיה וישך אותה ותמת, And she ordered that אפעה ephe be brought to her; applied to her breasts, it killed her with its bite. Ephe, that is, the asp. For the common run of writers holds that Cleopatra was bitten by an asp. Strabo, book 17: Ἑαυτὴν ἐν τῇ φρουρᾷ διεχειρίσατο λάθρα δήγματι ἀσπίδος [Heautēn en tē phroura diecheirisato lathra dēgmati aspidos]; She secretly killed herself in custody by the bite of an asp. Velleius Paterculus, book 2: Cleopatra, having eluded her guards, had an asp brought in and, free of a woman's fear, gave up her breath at its bite. Suetonius in Augustus: She was thought to have died from the bite of an asp. Plutarch in Antony: Λέγεται δὲ τὴν ἀσπίδα κομισθῆναι σὺν τοῖς σύκοις [Legetai de tēn aspida komisthēnai syn tois sykois], etc. καὶ τὸν βραχίονα παρασχεῖν τῷ δήγματι γυμνώσασαν [kai ton brachiona paraschein tō dēgmati gymnōsasan]; [III, 126] They say that the asp was brought in with the figs, etc., and that she bared her arm and offered it to the bite. Again: Οἱ δὲ τηρεῖσθαι μὲν ἐν ὑδρίᾳ τὴν ἀσπίδα καθειργμένην φάσκουσιν [Hoi de tēreisthai men en hydria tēn aspida katheirgmenēn phaskousin]. Others say that the asp was kept shut up in a jar. [col. 359] And below: Οἷς ἔοικε πιστεύσας καὶ ὁ Καῖσαρ· ἐν γὰρ τῷ θριάμβῳ τῆς Κλεοπάτρας αὐτῆς εἴδωλον ἐκομίζετο, καὶ τῆς ἀσπίδος ἐμπεφυκυίας [Hois eoike pisteusas kai ho Kaisar; en gar tō thriambō tēs Kleopatras autēs eidōlon ekomizeto, kai tēs aspidos empephykuias]. Caesar seems to have believed them, since in the triumph an image of Cleopatra was carried, with asps fastened to it. Aelian, History, book 9, chapter 11: Τὸ τῆς ἀσπίδος δῆγμα πρᾳότατον εἶναι ἤλεγξε Κλεόπατρα [To tēs aspidos dēgma praotaton einai ēlenxe Kleopatra]; Cleopatra proved that the bite of the asp is the gentlest. And in chapter 61, after saying that the bite of the asp is scarcely detectable, because the poison lies hidden inside and is not spread over the surface: Ἔνθεν τοι καὶ τῆς Κλεοπάτρας ὁ θάνατος τοῖς ἀμφὶ τὸν Σεβαστὸν οὐ πάνυ τι ῥᾳδίως ἐγνώσθη [Enthen toi kai tēs Kleopatras ho thanatos tois amphi ton Sebaston ou pany ti rhadiōs egnōsthē]; Hence it is that the death of Cleopatra was not easily recognized by those around Augustus. Dio in Augustus: Ἀπέθανεν, ἀσπίδος αὐτῇ ἐν ὑδρίᾳ εἰσκομισθείσης [Apethanen, aspidos autē en hydria eiskomistheisēs]. She died, an asp having been brought to her in a jar. Galen, To Piso on Theriac, book 1, chapter 8, after treating the species of asps: Τούτων γοῦν φασι τῶν θηρίων τινὶ τὴν βασιλίδα Κλεοπάτραν, βουληθεῖσαν λαθεῖν τοὺς φυλάττοντας, ταχέως τε, καὶ ἀνυπόπτως ἀποθανεῖν [Toutōn goun phasi tōn thēriōn tini tēn basilida Kleopatran, boulētheisan lathein tous phylattontas, tacheōs te, kai anypoptōs apothanein]; They say, then, that by one of these beasts Queen Cleopatra, wishing to escape the notice of her guards, brought death on herself quickly and without suspicion. Tertullian, To the Martyrs, chapter 4: A woman willingly sought out beasts, and indeed asp serpents more horrid than a bull or a bear, which Cleopatra set upon herself so as not to fall into the hands of her enemy. Sextus Aurelius Victor, On Illustrious Men, under Cleopatra: When she pretended to bring funeral offerings to him (Antony) in his Mausoleum, she died by applying asps. Eutropius, book 7: Cleopatra let an asp at herself and was killed by its poison. Solinus: There are many different species of asps, but unequal in their effects for harm. The dipsas kills by thirst. The hypnale, because it kills by sleep, is bought for death, as Cleopatra also testifies. Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, chapter 4: The hypnalis, a kind of asp so called because it kills by sleep. This Cleopatra applied to herself, and so was released by death as if by sleep. Clearly, then, for the Hebrew writer אפעה ephe, which killed Cleopatra by its bite, is the asp. Likewise in Eutychius of Alexandria the same Cleopatra ordered those famous maidservants ان ياتياها بالافعا التي تسي بالاسغيدة [an yaʾtiyāhā bi-l-afʿā allatī tusī bi-l-asghīda] to bring her the ephe which they call the asp. For so one must read instead of the corrupt word بالاسيليدة [bi-l-asīlīda]. So in Job 20:16. לשון אפעה, the tongue of the ephe, is in the Syriac ܠܫܢܐ ܕܐܣܦܣ [לשנא דאספס], the tongue of the asp. And in Isa 30:6 the same version again has ܐܣܦܣ [אספס], asp, for אפעה ephe, and the Greeks ἀσπίδες [aspides].

But others render it βασιλίσκον [basiliskon], or regulus, as Jerome does, and those same Greeks at Isa 59:5. Others render it ἔχιδναν [echidnan], viper, as Aquila does, and the same Jerome in [III, 127] Job and at Isa 30:6. The Chaldee sometimes has תנינא, dragon, sometimes חיון, serpent, sometimes חרמנין מפרחין, flying snakes. And the Syriac in one place has ܚܘܝܘܢܐ [חויונא], little snake, and the Arabic الحية الجردا [al-ḥayya al-jardā] smooth serpent, which is also called by another name, الاقرع [al-aqraʿ] bald. Hence Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: الاقرع من الحيات متعط شعر راسه لكثرة سمه [al-aqraʿ min al-ḥayyāt mutamaʿʿiṭ shaʿr raʾsihi li-kathrat summihi] The bald one among serpents is the one that is stripped of the hair of its head because of the abundance of its poison. Thus hardly anything certain about this word can be drawn from the ancient versions of Scripture.

Among the masters of the Hebrews there is the same hesitation here. אפעה ephe is rendered by Solomon on Job as burning serpent, that is, prester; by Mordecai and Pomarius [=David de Pomis, Ṣemaḥ David (Venice 1587)] as the serpent which infects by its look alone, that is, the regulus or basilisk. That [col. 360] Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim] was of this opinion one might gather from the fact that on Es. XXX he makes אפעה ephe and צפעוני tsiphoni synonyms. Yet he seems rather to mean the cenchrites, since elsewhere the same author describes אפעה ephe as a serpent with a variegated and spotted skin, following the opinion of R. Meir, which rests on the authority of the Chaldee paraphrase, where אפעיא stand for הצבועים, that is, as some would have it, painted and spotted serpents, 1 Sam 13:18. I pass over the trifles of the Talmudists: that in the carob tree, every seventieth year, two serpents of this species are generated, one of each sex, the male being called צבוע and the female נפרוא, and that nature stops here as if by deliberate design, so that this plague may not grow worse through excessive loss of life.

In this crowd of interpreters I do not doubt that the laurel must go to Aquila, for whom אפעה ephe is the viper. Many of the more recent scholars rightly follow him, since it is a well-established fact that even today among the Arabs الافعي [al-afʿī] alephe means viper. This is clear not only from the Arabic paraphrase of the New Testament, in which الافعي [al-afʿī] alephe, that is, the viper, fastens itself on Paul's hand, Acts 28:3, and the Pharisees are repeatedly ^{a)} called اولاد الافاعي [awlād al-afāʿī] offspring of alaphai, that is, of vipers, but also from the books of the physicians. Thus Avicenna [=Ibn Sīnā, al-Qānūn fī l-ṭibb (the Canon)], in book 2 of the Canon, prescribes ابوجلسا [abūjalsā] or شنجار [shinjār] anchusa, and اناجلس [anājalis] anagallis, and لوف [lūf] dracontium, and كرسنة [kirsanna] bitter vetch, and قسط [qusṭ] costus, and حسك [ḥasak] caltrop, and كرم [karm] the vine, and فاشرا [fāshirā] bryony, and بول الانسان [bawl al-insān] human urine against the bite of الافاعي [al-afāʿī] alaphai, that is, of vipers. For all these are taken from Dioscorides, who recommends the same remedies for ἐχιοδήκτοις [echiodēktois]. The same Avicenna reports ^{b)} that the fat of [III, 128] الافعي [al-afʿī] alephe is an effective remedy against dimness of the eyes, and he orders its flesh to be used for the treatment of leprosy ^{c)}. These very powers are attributed to the flesh and fat of the viper by Dioscorides, Galen, Paul and Aëtius. Finally, that the word افعي [afʿī] ephe is used for the viper will be clearer than daylight to anyone who compares the writings of the Greeks with Avicenna's treatises On leprosy, On theriac, and On the bite of الافاعي [al-afāʿī] alaphai ^{R1}.

Particular note should be taken of what pertains to the description. Thus Avicenna, book 5, p. 179, in the chapter entitled صنعة اقراص الافاعي [ṣanʿat aqrāṣ al-afāʿī] The art of the troches of alaphai, that is, of vipers, says: الافاعي هي الحياة المفرطحة الرووس المستعرضتها خصوصا عند قرب الرقبة الدقاق رقابها جدا البتر اذنابها الفحاحة الكشاشة وليس يصلح لهذا الاقراص كل الافاعي بل الشقر ومن الشقر الاناث وعلامتها ان الذكر [col. 361] في كل شدق ناب واحد وللاناث اكثر من ناب واحد [al-afāʿī hiya al-ḥayyāt al-mufarṭaḥat al-ruʾūs al-mustaʿriḍatuhā khuṣūṣan ʿinda qurb al-raqaba al-diqāq riqābuhā jiddan al-butr adhnābuhā al-faḥḥāḥat al-kashshāsha wa-laysa yaṣluḥu li-hādhā al-aqrāṣ kull al-afāʿī bal al-shuqr wa-min al-shuqr al-ināth wa-ʿalāmatuhā anna al-dhakar fī kull shidq nāb wāḥid wa-li-l-ināth akthar min nāb wāḥid] Alaphai (vipers) are serpents with flat heads, very broad especially around the neck, with a very slender neck, a truncated tail, a clear hiss, and a noisy gait. Yet not all الافاعي [al-afāʿī] alaphai (vipers) are good for these troches, but the red ones, and of the red ones the females. Their mark is that, whereas the male has one canine tooth on each side of the jaw, the female has several ^{R2}. Hence the same author, book 4, in the chapter في [III, 129] لسع الافاعي [fī lasʿ al-afāʿī] On the bite of alaphai (vipers), Arab. p. 137, Lat. Fen 6, tract. 3, ch. 32: لسع الانثي تعرف بوجود مغارز لاكثر من نابين في الجهة التي عض بها [lasʿ al-unthā tuʿrafu bi-wujūd maghāriz li-akthar min nābayn fī al-jiha allatī ʿaḍḍa bihā] The bite of the female is recognized from the fact that more than two canine teeth are found to have been driven into the part which it attacked with its bite. Everyone can see that this belongs to the description of the viper, about which Aelian, book 10 of the Hist., ch. 9, says: Νίκανδρος δέ φησιν, ἐκ μὲν τοῦ δήγματος, ὅπερ οὖν ὁ ἔχις ἐμφύει, δύο ὀδόντων ἴχνη φαίνεσθαι· πλέον δὲ, εἰ δάκοι ἡ ἔχιδνα. [Nikandros de phēsin, ek men tou dēgmatos, hoper oun ho echis emphyei, dyo odontōn ichnē phainesthai; pleon de, ei dakoi hē echidna.] Nicander says that from the bite which the echis (that is, the male viper) inflicts, the marks of two teeth appear; but more when the echidna bites, that is, the female viper: which is to be understood of the canines. For so Nicander in the Theriaca, verse 231:
Τοῦ μὲν ὑπὲρ κυνόδοντε δύο χροῒ τεκμαίρονται Ἰὸν ἐρευγόμενοι· πλέονες δέ τοι αἰὲν ἐχίδνης· [Tou men hyper kynodonte dyo chroi tekmairontai / Ion ereugomenoi; pleones de toi aien echidnēs;]

Him (the echis) two canine teeth (impressed) in the body betray, belching out poison; but the echidna (that is, the female viper) always more. And Galen, book 2, On Theriac, ch. 13: Τούτῳ γὰρ τοῦ ἄῤῥενος ἡ ἔχιδνα διήνεγκε τῷ πλέονας τῶν δύο κυνοδόντων ἔχειν· [Toutō gar tou arrhenos hē echidna diēnenke tō pleonas tōn dyo kynodontōn echein;] For in this the female viper differs from the male, that it has more than two canine teeth. Κυνόδους [Kynodous], canine tooth, is in Arabic ناب [nāb], the word which Avicenna uses. Further, on the viper's broad head, slender neck, truncated tail and yellow colour, see Galen and Aëtius; from whom, however, Avicenna differs in that he attributes to vipers in general what they attribute only to the female.

It should moreover be noted that in Abenbitar [=Ibn al-Bayṭār] the whole chapter of Dioscorides On the flesh of the viper is referred to افعى [afʿā] ephe. And these words of his, Ἐχίδνης σὰρξ ἑψηθεῖσα, καὶ ἐσθιομένη, ὀξυδερκεῖς ποιεῖ τὰς ὄψεις [Echidnēs sarx hepsētheisa, kai esthiomenē, oxyderkeis poiei tas opseis], are rendered in Arabic thus: لحم الافاعي اذا طبخ واكل يحد البصر [laḥm al-afāʿī idhā ṭubikha wa-ukila yuḥiddu al-baṣar] The flesh of alaphai, cooked and eaten, sharpens the sight. Again, to these words of the Greek text, Κατασκευάζονται δὲ καὶ ἅλες ἐξ αὐτῶν πρὸς [III, 130] τὰ αὐτὰ, πλὴν οὐχ᾽ ὁμοίως ἐνεργοῦσι [Kataskeuazontai de kai hales ex autōn pros ta auta, plēn ouch homoiōs energousi], correspond these Arabic ones: وقد يعمل ملح من لحوم الافاعي يفعل فعل الافاعي غير انه انقص فعلا منه [wa-qad yuʿmalu milḥ min luḥūm al-afāʿī yafʿalu fiʿl al-afāʿī ghayr annahu anqaṣ fiʿlan minhu] A salt is also made from the flesh of alaphai, which has the same effect as alaphai, except that it is of lesser efficacy. In the same place the Greek reads: Καθίεται δὲ ἔχιδνα ζῶσα εἰς καινὴν χύτραν· [Kathietai de echidna zōsa eis kainēn chytran;] and the Arabic: توخذ افعي حية وتصير في قدر جديدة [tuʾkhadhu afʿā ḥayya wa-tuṣayyaru fī qidr jadīda] An ephe is taken alive and put into a new pot [col. 362]. In the same Abenbitar a lengthy passage of Galen is cited, in which it is shown that lepers are healed by eating viper's flesh. Its beginning is as follows: لحوم الافاعي تجدها عيانا تسخن وتجفف البدن اذا هي طيبت كما يطيب لحم المرماهي بالزيت والملح والشبث والكراث والما بمقدار قصد [luḥūm al-afāʿī tajiduhā ʿiyānan tusakhkhinu wa-tujaffifu al-badan idhā hiya ṭuyyibat kamā yuṭayyabu laḥm al-marmāhī bi-l-zayt wa-l-milḥ wa-l-shibith wa-l-kurrāth wa-l-māʾ bi-miqdār qaṣd] You will plainly find that the flesh of alaphai (vipers) warms and dries the body, when it is seasoned like eels, with oil, salt, dill, leek, and a suitable measure of water. This reads thus in Greek in On Simple Medicines, book 2, ch. 1: Τὰς γοῦν τῶν ἐχιδνῶν θερμαινούσας τε, καὶ ξηραινούσας, ἐναργῶς ἐστιν ἰδεῖν ἀρτυομένας, ὥσπερ αἱ ἐγχέλεις, ἐλαίῳ, καὶ ἁλσὶ, καὶ ἀνήθῳ, καὶ πράσῳ, καὶ ὕδατι, δηλονότι κατὰ τοῦ συμμέτρου. [Tas goun tōn echidnōn thermainousas te, kai xērainousas, enargōs estin idein artyomenas, hōsper hai encheleis, elaiō, kai halsi, kai anēthō, kai prasō, kai hydati, dēlonoti kata tou symmetrou.] See the rest there.

In Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt] it is said of الافعي [al-afʿā] alephe: قد اظلمت عيناها تطلب شجرة الرازيانج وتحك عينها بها يرجع اليها ضوها [qad aẓlamat ʿaynāhā taṭlubu shajarat al-rāziyānaj wa-taḥukku ʿaynahā bihā yarjiʿu ilayhā ḍawʾuhā] When its eyes are blinded, it seeks fennel to rub them with, so as to recover its sight. Indeed, in Andromachus' poem On the composition of pastilles from vipers, these serpents are described, around the beginning of spring,
Διζόμενοι χλωροῦ σπέρμα λαβεῖν μαράθρου, ᾽Οξυτέρην τὸ τίθησιν ἐφ᾽ ἑρπυστῆρσιν ὀπωπήν· [Dizomenoi chlōrou sperma labein marathrou, / Oxyterēn to tithēsin eph' herpystērsin opōpēn;]

Taking pains to obtain the seed of green fennel, which makes the sight of these reptiles sharper. This Zamachsari, in the manner of the Arabs, exaggerates as follows: الافعي اذا اتت عليها الف سنة عميت وقد الهمها الله ان تمسح عينيها بورق الرازيانج الرطب فيرد اليها بصرها وربما كانت في برية وبينها وبين الريف مسيرة ثلثه ايام فتطوي تلك المسافة علي طولها وعلي عماها هتي تهجم في بعض البساتين علي شجر الرازيانج لا تخطيه فتحك به عينها [III, 131] فترجع باصرة باذن الله تعالي [al-afʿī idhā atat ʿalayhā alf sana ʿamiyat wa-qad alhamahā Allāh an tamsaḥa ʿaynayhā bi-waraq al-rāziyānaj al-raṭb fa-yaruddu ilayhā baṣarahā wa-rubbamā kānat fī bariyya wa-baynahā wa-bayna al-rīf masīrat thalatha ayyām fa-taṭwī tilka al-masāfa ʿalā ṭūlihā wa-ʿalā ʿamāhā hatā tahjum fī baʿḍ al-basātīn ʿalā shajar al-rāziyānaj lā tukhṭīhi fa-taḥukku bihi ʿaynahā fa-tarjiʿu bāṣiratan bi-idhn Allāh taʿālā] Alephe (the viper), when it has lived a thousand years, is blinded; and God inspires it to anoint its eyes with a leaf of fresh fennel, so that its sight may be restored. And sometimes it is in a desert which lies three days' journey from cultivated land; it traverses this whole distance, however great it is, until it comes upon fennel in some garden, and it does not stray from it; and when it has [col. 363] rubbed its eyes with it, it recovers its sight, by the grace of God.

Many of the ancients tell the tale that vipers copulate by the mouth, and that in the heat of coition the female bites off the male's head. Herodotus, book 3, ch. 109: Ἐπεὰν θορνύωνται κατὰ ζεύγεα, καὶ ἐν αὐτῇ ᾖ ὁ ἔρσην τῇ ἐκποιήσει, ἀπιεμένου αὐτοῦ τὴν γονὴν, ἡ θήλεα ἅπτεται τῆς δειρῆς, καὶ ἐμφῦσα οὐκ ἀνίει πρὶν ἂν διαφάγῃ· ὁ μὲν δὲ ἔρσην ἀποθνήσκει τρόπῳ τῷ εἰρημένῳ. [Epean thornyōntai kata zeugea, kai en autē ē ho ersēn tē ekpoiēsei, apiemenou autou tēn gonēn, hē thēlea haptetai tēs deirēs, kai emphysa ouk aniei prin an diaphagē; ho men de ersēn apothnēskei tropō tō eirēmenō.] When they couple in pairs, and the male is in the very act and emits his seed, the female, clinging tightly to his neck, does not let go before she has devoured it; and the male indeed perishes in this way. Nicander, Theriaca, line 130:
Ἡνίκα, θορνυμένου ἔχιος, θολερῷ κυνόδοντι Θουρὰς ὀδὰξ ἐμφῦσα κάρην ἀπέκοψεν ὁμεύνου· [Hēnika, thornymenou echios, tholerō kynodonti Thouras odax emphysa karēn apekopsen homeunou;]

When the vigorous female, clinging with her teeth to the male as he couples, cut off her mate's head with her bold tooth. Pliny, ch. 10, ch. 62: Tightly embracing his neck, she cuts it off together with the head itself. Aelian, History, book 1, ch. 24: Ἐμφῦσα γὰρ αὐτοῦ τῷ τραχήλῳ, διακόπτει αὐτὸν αὐτῇ τῇ κεφαλῇ [Emphysa gar autou tō trachēlō, diakoptei auton autē tē kephalē] (read σὺν αὐτῇ τῇ κεφαλῇ [syn autē tē kephalē]). Galen, On Theriac to Piso, ch. 9: Φασὶ γὰρ αὐτὴν ἀνοίγουσαν τὸ στόμα πρὸς τὸ δέξασθαι τοῦ ἄῤῥενος τὸν θορὸν, μετὰ τὸ λαβεῖν, ἀποκόπτειν αὐτοῦ τὴν κεφαλήν· [Phasi gar autēn anoigousan to stoma pros to dexasthai tou arrhenos ton thoron, meta to labein, apokoptein autou tēn kephalēn;] For they say that she opens her mouth to receive the male's seed, and, having received it, bites off his head. Epiphanius also writes this in the Heresy of the Gnostics: Διὰ τοῦ στόματος χαινούσης τῆς θηλείας τὸν ἄῤῥενα τὴν κεφαλὴν εἰσβάλλειν· ἐκείνης δὲ πάθει συσχεθείσης, ἀποτέμνειν τὴν τούτου κεφαλήν· [Dia tou stomatos chainousēs tēs thēleias ton arrhena tēn kephalēn eisballein; ekeinēs de pathei syschetheisēs, apotemnein tēn toutou kephalēn;] That the male thrusts his head into the mouth of the gaping female; and she, roused by lust, cuts off his head. Prudentius, in the Hamartigenia, the first poem, line 588:

— — — the lewd female thirsts with gaping mouth for her husband, who is to die: he thrusts his three-tongued head into his mate's jaws, and, burning, enters her kisses, instilling the generative poison by the coupling of the mouth. The bride, wounded by the force of pleasure, breaks with her bite the swallowed throat of her lover amid the sweet compacts.

Isidore: It is said, moreover, that the male, having inserted his mouth, spits his seed into the viper. But she, turned to rage by the pleasure of lust, bites off the male's head, received into her mouth. But Eustathius says otherwise, p. 43 on the Hexaemeron: Φασὶ δὲ τὴν ἔχιδναν διὰ [III, 132] στόματος τοῦ ἄῤῥενος τὴν γονὴν δέχεσθαι, καὶ συναποκόπτειν τοῖς ὀδοῦσι αὐτὸ τὸ μόριον, καὶ ἀποκτείνειν αὐτόν· [Phasi de tēn echidnan dia stomatos tou arrhenos tēn gonēn dechesthai, kai synapokoptein tois odousi auto to morion, kai apokteinein auton;] They say that the viper receives the male's seed through the mouth, and, having cut off the member with her teeth, kills him. So also the Arabs in Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān]: ومن الافاعي ما يتسافد بافواهها فاذا وطى الذكر الانثي وقع مغشيا عليه فتعمد الانثي الي موضع مذاكيره فتقطعها نهشا فيموت من ساعته [wa-min al-afāʿī mā yatasāfad bi-afwāhihā fa-idhā waṭiʾa al-dhakar al-unthā waqaʿa maghshiyyan ʿalayhi fa-taʿmidu al-unthā ilā mawḍiʿ madhākīrihi fa-taqṭaʿuhā nahshan fa-yamūtu min sāʿatihi] There are some of the alaphai (vipers) that copulate by the mouth; and, after the male has covered the female, he falls into a swoon. Then the female, seeking out the place of his genitals, bites them off, and he dies on the spot ^{R3}.

These and other things show more than enough that the אפעה of the Hebrews and the افعى [afʿā] of the Arabs is the viper. Nor is the reason for the name obscure. For in Hebrew פעה means to cry out with a strained voice: hence, therefore, the viper is called אפעה. Avicenna above ^{d)} attributes to it الفحيحة [al-faḥīḥa], that is, a clear hiss. And the Italian mountebanks, on the testimony of Massario in Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], call it suffili from its horrible hissing, because, when it is harassed, it gives out such hisses that they are heard a stone's throw away. Further, it is likely that these hisses are strained most of all in giving birth, because it is then afflicted with the sharpest pain. And this is properly פעה. For the verb פעה is not used of just any cry, [col. 364] but of the cry in childbirth. Thus Isa 42:14. כיולדה אפעה, like a woman in labour I will cry out ^{R4}. Hence the Hebrews hold that the Egyptian midwife in Exod 1:15 was called פועה, because she was customarily called upon with such wailing of women in labour. Accordingly אפעה ephe properly signifies that kind of serpent from which the pains of birth wring a more violent hiss ^{R5}. This fits the viper above all. Not because its young come out by gnawing through their mother's belly, as the ancients believed. For Theophrastus rightly rejected this as fabulous, and after him Aelian, History book 15, ch. 16. But neither is it certain, as they maintain, that its womb is burst during birth itself because of its narrowness. Certainly the Philosopher does not say that the womb bursts in birth, but the membranes in which the young are wrapped. His words are in the History, book 5, chapter 34: Τίκτει δὲ [III, 133] μικρὰ ἐχίδια ἐν ὑμέσιν, οἳ περιῤῥήγνυνται τριταῖοι [Tiktei de mikra echidia en hymesin, hoi perirrhēgnyntai tritaioi]· It gives birth to small vipers in membranes, which break on the third day. But what follows gave occasion to the fiction: Ἐνίοτε δὲ καὶ ἔσωθεν διαφαγόντα αὐτὰ ἐξέρχεται [Eniote de kai esōthen diaphagonta auta exerchetai]· Sometimes also, while they are inside, they gnaw through (not the mother's womb, but the membranes he had mentioned) and come out by themselves. Yet the viper's birth is more difficult for this reason, that it bears live young, whereas the other serpents only hatch eggs. Hence it is called vipera [viper], either as if vi pariat [it gives birth by force], or rather because it is vivipara [viviparous]. From this it is now abundantly clear that אפעה ephe is the viper. And so this rendering fits well enough the three passages of Scripture in which that word occurs, as will be evident to anyone who runs through them.
The first is Job 20:16. תהרגהו לשון אפעה, The tongue of the ephe shall kill him, that is, of the viper, whose bites are deadly even to the hugest beasts. Ovid, book 2 On the Remedy of Love:
The little viper kills the massive bull with its bite.

And in the words The tongue of the ephe shall kill him, what properly belongs to the teeth is attributed to the tongue, because the serpent bites with its tongue thrust out, as if the tongue inflicted the wound. Hence Seneca in Medea 686:
— — — the serpent drags its immense body, and thrusts out its three-forked tongue, and seeks those to whom it may come bringing death. — — — —

And Kimchi on these words of Psalm 140, They have sharpened their tongue like a serpent: חדדו לשונם לדבר רעות כמו הנחש שמחדד לשונו בשבא לנשוך, They have sharpened their tongue to speak evil, as the serpent sharpens its tongue when it prepares to bite.

The second passage is Isa 30:6, where among the Egyptian beasts are reckoned אפעה ושרף מעופף, the ephe and the flying hydrus. For as Egypt nourishes every kind of serpent, so also vipers in great numbers. Ammianus, book 22: Egypt also nourishes countless serpents, raging beyond all deadliness: basilisks, and amphisbaenas, and scytales, and acontiases, and dipsases, and vipers. Indeed the Egyptian vipers have something peculiar. Accordingly Belon [=Pierre Belon, Observations (1553)] describes them specifically in Observations, book 2, ch. 54.

The third passage is Isa 59:5. He who eats of their eggs will die; והזורה תבקע אפעה, and what is crushed, out of it will burst forth an ephe, or viper. What is crushed] In Hebrew הזורה is said here of an egg, as in Job 39:18 of the ostrich's egg: She forgets that a foot תזורה may crush it, and the beast of the field trample it. You will object that eggs cannot be attributed to the viper, because the viper is not ὠοτόκος [ōotokos], oviparous, but ζωοτόκος [zōotokos], viviparous, as we have already noted in passing. And Aristotle expressly [III, 134] asserts it, History book 1, ch. 6: Ἀλλ᾽ οἱ μὲν ἄλλοι ὠοτοκοῦσιν ὄφεις, ἡ δ᾽ ἔχιδνα μόνον ζωοτοκεῖ [All' hoi men alloi ōotokousin opheis, hē d' echidna monon zōotokei]· The other serpents lay eggs, but the viper alone bears a live animal. And Nicander, Theriaca, line 135:
Οἵη γὰρ βαρύθει ὑπὸ κύματι, τοὶ δὲ καθ᾽ ὕλην Ὠοτόκοι ὄφιες λεπυρὴν θάλπουσι γενέθλην. [Hoiē gar barythei hypo kymati, toi de kath' hylēn Ōotokoi ophies lepyrēn thalpousi genethlēn.]

For she alone is heavy with young, while the other serpents, being oviparous, brood their offspring in the woods, enclosed in a shell. [col. 365] And Aelian, book 1, ch. 24: Τίκτει δὲ οὐκ ὠὰ, ἀλλὰ βρέφη, καὶ ἔστιν ἐνεργὰ ἤδη τὴν φύσιν αὐτῶν τὴν κακίστην· [Tiktei de ouk ōa, alla brephē, kai estin energa ēdē tēn physin autōn tēn kakistēn] But she bears not eggs but young, in which that most evil nature already shows itself. And Suidas: Ἔχις· εἶδος ὄφεως, ἀπὸ τοῦ κατέχειν, διότι μόνον τῶν ὄφεων οὐκ ὠοτοκεῖ, ἀλλὰ ζωοτοκεῖ· [Echis; eidos opheōs, apo tou katechein, dioti monon tōn opheōn ouk ōotokei, alla zōotokei] The viper, a kind of serpent, named from holding in (because it holds its young in the womb), because it alone of the serpents bears not eggs but a living animal. I reply that the viper, although it brings forth a living animal, nevertheless produces an egg inside, from which that animal comes forth. The Philosopher, On the Generation of Animals, book 1, ch. 10: Οἱ ἔχεις θύραζε μὲν ζωοτοκοῦσιν, ἐν αὐτοῖς δὲ ὠοτοκοῦσι πρῶτον, ὠοτοκοῦσι δὲ τέλειον ὠόν· οὕτως γὰρ γεννᾶται ἐκ τοῦ ὠοῦ τὸ ζῶον. [Hoi echeis thyraze men zōotokousin, en autois de ōotokousi prōton, ōotokousi de teleion ōon; houtōs gar gennatai ek tou ōou to zōon] Vipers indeed bring forth a living animal outwardly, but first they produce an egg within themselves, and that a perfect one: for thus the animal is generated from the egg. The same, History, book 3, ch. 3: Τὰ μὲν γὰρ ἄλλα γένη τῶν ὄφεων ὠοτοκεῖ· ἔχις δὲ ζωοτοκεῖ μόνον, ὠοτοκήσας ἐν αὑτῷ πρῶτον. [Ta men gar alla genē tōn opheōn ōotokei; echis de zōotokei monon, ōotokēsas en hautō prōton] The other kinds of serpents lay eggs; the viper alone generates a living animal, after first producing eggs within itself. And book 5, at the end: Τῶν δὲ ὄφεων ὁ μὲν ἔχεις ἔξω ζωοτοκεῖ, ἐν αὑτῷ πρῶτον ὠοτοκήσας· τὸ δὲ ὠὸν, ὥσπερ τῶν ἰχθύων, μονόχρουν ἐστὶ, καὶ μαλακόδερμον. [Tōn de opheōn ho men echeis exō zōotokei, en hautō prōton ōotokēsas; to de ōon, hōsper tōn ichthyōn, monochroun esti, kai malakodermon] Of the serpents the viper alone brings forth a living animal, having first produced eggs within itself; and its egg is of one color and soft, like those of fishes. Hence Pliny says of the viper: Of land animals she alone produces within herself eggs of one color and soft, like fishes. Some affirm this very thing from Theophrastus, History of Plants, book 7, ch. 14, where, after saying that τὴν ἀπαρίνην [tēn aparinēn], cleavers, produces a flower not visible but hidden within, he adds: ὥστε παρόμιον εἶναι τὸ συμβαῖνον, ὥσπερ ἐπὶ τῶν γαλεῶν, καὶ τῶν κρηνῶν· ἐκεῖνά τε γὰρ ἐν ἑαυτοῖς ὠοτοκήσαντα ζωογονεῖ· [hōste paromion einai to symbainon, hōsper epi tōn galeōn, kai tōn krēnōn; ekeina te gar en heautois ōotokēsanta zōogonei] which Gaza rendered thus: So that it is like what happens in dogfish and vipers: for these, once they have produced eggs within themselves, presently give birth to living animals. That is, for the corrupt word κρηνῶν [krēnōn] he wanted to read ἐχιδνῶν [echidnōn]. I would prefer κυνῶν [kynōn] or ῥίνων [rhinōn]. If you follow the former, γαλεῶν [galeōn] and κυνῶν [kynōn] will be synonyms, and after τῶν γαλεῶν [tōn galeōn] Theophrastus will have added καὶ τῶν κυνῶν [kai tōn kynōn] by way of distinction, so that we might know that by the name τῶν γαλεῶν [tōn galeōn] are meant κύνας [kynas], sea-dogs, which are also called γαλεοὶ [galeoi]. But if for τῶν κρηνῶν [tōn krēnōn] you read τῶν ῥίνων [tōn rhinōn], angel sharks will be understood, which Oppian counts among the kinds of dogfish in these words, Halieutica, book 1, line 379:

[III, 135] — — — γαλεῶν δ' ἑτερότροπα φῦλα, Σκύμνοι, καὶ λείαι, καὶ ἀκανθίαι, ἐν δ' ἄρα τοῖσι 'Ρῖναι. — — — — — [galeōn d' heterotropa phyla, Skymnoi, kai leiai, kai akanthiai, en d' ara toisi Rhinai]

But there are diverse kinds of dogfish: scymni, and leae, and acanthiae; among these too are the angel sharks. Accordingly the Philosopher says that dogfish and angel sharks have this in common, that they receive their young within themselves and emit them, History, book 6, ch. 10. On this very point Oppian compares dogfish and angel sharks with one another, in line 742 of the same book. But whatever you read in Theophrastus, it is clear from Aristotle and Pliny that eggs are rightly attributed to the viper too, although she has them within herself and hidden in the womb: so that no one should find it strange that Isaiah spoke of the eggs of the viper.

Although it is by no means necessary to understand the viper precisely in that place. For even though אפעה ephe properly means the viper, as what we have taught so far amply proves, it is nevertheless certain that among the Arabs the word افعي [afʿī] ephe extends much more widely. This is proved by the following words of Avicenna, Canon book 4, Fen 4, tract. 3, ch. 3, which is On the Cure of Leprosy: ولا يجب ان تكون الافعي سبخية او ريغية ولا رقية ولا شطية فانها في الاكثر قليلة المنفعة ولكثير منها غاياة التعطيش والاتلاف به [wa-lā yajibu an takūna al-afʿī sabakhiyya aw rīghiyya wa-lā raqqiyya wa-lā shaṭṭiyya fa-innahā fī al-akthar qalīlat al-manfaʿa wa-li-kathīr minhā ghāyāt al-taʿṭīsh wa-al-itlāf bihi] [col. 366] بل تختار الجبلية لاسيما البيض [bal tukhtār al-jabaliyya lā siyyamā al-bīḍ] The alephe (viper) should not be from salty places, or muddy ones, or riverbanks, or seashores; for such a one is, for the most part, of little efficacy. Above all, among these the one that excites a deadly thirst (the dipsas) is fatal. Let a mountain one therefore be chosen, especially a white one, etc. And in book 5, in the chapter On Troches made from Viper's Flesh: وليس يصلح لهذه الاقراص كل الافاعي بل شقر [wa-laysa yaṣluḥu li-hādhihi al-aqrāṣ kull al-afāʿī bal shuqr] Not all alaphai are suitable for these troches, but only the yellow ones, etc. And a little later: ويجب ان تجتنب الضارنة والرقم والرقش الضارية الي البياض ولا تصطاد من السباخ وشطوط الاودية الانهار والبحار ولا المشجرة فان فيها البلوطية الخبيثة المعطشة [wa-yajibu an tujtanaba al-ḍārina wa-al-ruqm wa-al-ruqsh al-ḍāriya ilā al-bayāḍ wa-lā tuṣṭād min al-sibākh wa-shuṭūṭ al-awdiya al-anhār wa-al-biḥār wa-lā al-mushajjara fa-inna fīhā al-ballūṭiyya al-khabītha al-muʿṭisha] And the horned ones (vipers) must be rejected, and the variegated or two-coloured ones tending toward white. Nor should they be sought from salty places, or the banks of torrents and rivers, and the shores of seas; nor from trees, because in them are the dryini, foul and thirst-exciting. And in the chapter On the Species of Serpents, which is book 4, Fen 6, tract. 3, ch. 21: والطبقة الثانية من الافاعي ونحوها ايضا مختلفة منها الافاعي الاصلية ومنها الافاعي البدوطية ومنها [III, 136] المعطشة وساير ما نذكر [wa-al-ṭabaqa al-thāniya min al-afāʿī wa-naḥwihā ayḍan mukhtalifa minhā al-afāʿī al-aṣliyya wa-minhā al-afāʿī al-badūṭiyya wa-minhā al-muʿṭisha wa-sāyir mā nadhkuru] The second order is that of the alaphai (or vipers) and similar creatures, whose species are diverse. For among them are alaphai ῥιζίαι [rhiziai], that is, those living in the roots of trees; likewise alaphai dryinae, and thirst-exciting ones, and the rest, which we shall mention. That is, according to the teaching of the Arabs there are three orders of serpents. The first contains those whose bite rejects all medicine and kills within three hours. The second, those that are treated by vomiting and by eating salted foods, and that bring death only on the third day after the bite. The third, those whose bite is not usually lethal, and is treated only by external remedies and by binding the affected part, so that the poison does not creep further. Further, since vipers are the best known in that second order of serpents, it came about that the name of vipers was common to all serpents of the same order. Therefore the Hebrew אפעה ephe, although it properly means the viper, could nevertheless, like the Arabic أفعى [afʿā], extend more widely; and hence it happens that interpreters pull this word apart into such diverse meanings. Nor were the Hebrews or the Arabs alone in so stretching the name of the viper: for in Aëtius the dipsas is defined as a species of viper that is found more in coastal places. And in Antipater of Sidon, Anthology book 3, ch. 16:
— — — — διψὰς ἔχιδνα Σαρκὶ τὸν ἐκ γενύων πικρὸν ἐνεῖσα χόλον, [— — — — dipsas echidna Sarki ton ek genyōn pikron eneisa cholon,] [col. 367]
the dipsas viper, injecting into the flesh the bitter poison from its jaws. And Nazianzen, Iamb. 22:
Διψὰς τίς ἐστι τῶν ἐχιδναίων γενῶν, [Dipsas tis esti tōn echidnaiōn genōn,]

There is a certain dipsas of the viper kind. Galen too, On Simples book 11, ch. 1, mentions vipers with the surname διψάδων [dipsadōn], by which τοὺς δηχθέντας φασὶν οὐκ ἐμπίπλασθαι πίνοντας, ἀλλὰ διαῤῥήγνυσθαι πρότερον, ἢ παύσασθαι διψῶντας [tous dēchthentas phasin ouk empiplasthai pinontas, alla diarrhēgnysthai proteron, ē pausasthai dipsōntas], they say those bitten are never sated by drinking, but burst in the middle before their thirst is allayed. It is evident that dipsades are described, which are taken for vipers because of the similarity of form. For, as Lucian asserts in the Dipsads, ἡ διψὰς ἐστιν ὄφις οὐ πάνυ μέγας, ἐχίδνῃ ὅμοιος [hē dipsas estin ophis ou pany megas, echidnē homoios], the dipsas is a serpent not very large, similar to a viper. And Nicander, Theriaca, verse 266:
Ναὶ μὴν δίψαδος εἶδος ὁμώσεται αἰὲν ἐχίδνῃ, [Nai mēn dipsados eidos homōsetai aien echidnē,]

Truly the form of the dipsas always resembles the viper's. The cerastes too, Gesner writes, is reckoned by many among the species of viper, evidently for the same reason. For the same Nicander describes it, verse 259:
Ἠΰτ᾽ ἔχιν· τῷ γάρ τε δομὴν ἰνδάλλεται ἴσην, [Ēyt᾽ echin; tō gar te domēn indalletai isēn,]

Like a viper; for its body appears similar to it. And in the Suda, under the word Ἔχις [Echis]: Λέγεται καὶ αἱμόῤῥους γένος ἔχεως [Legetai kai haimorrhous genos echeōs]; The haemorrhous is also said to be a kind of viper. This is [III, 137] taken from Aelian, book 15, ch. 13. Thus the hydra overcome by Hercules is called by some ἔχιδνα [echidna], that is, viper. Hence Hercules, when Achelous had been changed into a serpent, in Ovid's Metamorphoses book 9:
What fraction of the Lernaean viper will you, a single serpent, be?

So all write that the arrow with which Hercules killed Nessus was dipped in the poison of the Lernaean hydra; yet Diodorus, book 3, speaks of the same thus: Τῆς ἀκίδος τὸν ἐκ τῆς ἐχίδνης ἰὸν ἀνειληφυίας [Tēs akidos ton ek tēs echidnēs ion aneilēphuias]; Since the arrow had been imbued with the poison of the echidna (or viper). According to Homer, Iliad 2, verse 723, the Greeks left Philoctetes on the island of Lemnos
Ἕλκεϊ μοχθίζοντα κακῷ ὀλοόφρονος ὕδρου, [Helkei mochthizonta kakō oloophronos hydrou,]
Suffering from the evil ulcer of the deadly hydrus: but in the Philoctetes of Sophocles the Greeks expressed the same thing as
Πληγέντ᾽ ἐχίδνης ἀγρίῳ χαράγματι, [Plēgent᾽ echidnēs agriō charagmati,]

struck by the cruel wound of a viper. And Epiphanius too, in the Panarion, includes almost every kind of serpent under the genus of viper. Thus he compares the heresy of the Cerinthians τῇ καλουμένῃ σηπεδόνι ἐχίδνῃ [tē kaloumenē sēpedoni echidnē]. And he says that the heresy of the Secundians is trampled under the shoe of the gospel, ὡς μύαγρον ταύτην τὴν ἔχιδναν τὴν πολλαῖς ἑτέραις ἐχίδναις ἐοικυῖαν [hōs myagron tautēn tēn echidnan tēn pollais heterais echidnais eoikuian]. Likewise on the Marcosians: Διψάδα γάρ τινα ἔχιδνάν φασιν οἱ ἱστορήσαντες [Dipsada gar tina echidnan phasin hoi historēsantes], etc. And on the Colorbasians: Ὡς ἀπὸ ἀμφισβαίνης τῆς δικεφάλου ἐχίδνης [Hōs apo amphisbainēs tēs dikephalou echidnēs]. And on the Cataphrygians: Τῇ αἱμοῤῥοίᾳ ἐχίδνῃ ἐοικυῖα [Tē haimorrhoia echidnē eoikuia]. And on the Origenists: Ὥσπερ τὴν δεινὴν σκυτάλην, τὴν ἔχιδναν καλουμένην [Hōsper tēn deinēn skytalēn, tēn echidnan kaloumenēn]. And on Paul of Samosata: Δρυΐνας τις ἔχις οὕτω καλουμένη [Dryinas tis echis houtō kaloumenē]. From this it is evident that he regarded as vipers the sepedon, the myagrus, the dipsas, the amphisbaena, the haemorrhous, the scytale, the dryinus, and what not?

notes.text: Saadia puts this very افعي [afʿī] for the Hebrew אפעה in his Arabic translation of Isaiah, Chapter XXX, 6. LIX, 5. That افعي [afʿī] is the viper is also confirmed by the testimony of Forsskål [=Peter Forsskål, Descriptiones animalium (1775)], who in the Materia Medica Cahirina at the end of the Descriptio Animalium, p. 142, likewise has Vipera, with the Arabic name افعي [afʿī], Ephe, added. — Shaw [=Thomas Shaw, Travels (1738)] in his Travels, p. 159 of the German trans., mentions a serpent of the viper or snake kind, a foot long, whose colour varies with the soil in which it hides, called Leffah by the Arabs of western Africa. Oedmann [=Samuel Ödmann, Vermischte Sammlungen aus der Naturkunde] (Fasc. 4, Chapter 8, p. 79) thinks this name is the Arabic افعي [afʿī] itself with the article prefixed. But this opinion seems hardly probable to me, since Shaw states expressly that the name means to burn in Arabic. From this it is clear that it must be written in Arabic letters لفاح [laffāḥ], from لفح [lafaḥa], fire burned with its heat, poison with its sharpness, whence the adjective لافح [lāfiḥ] burning. The serpent's name لفّاح [laffāḥ], however, is not found in the lexicons.
notes.label: R1

notes.text: The أفعي [afʿī] of the Arabs is without doubt the Coluber Vipera of Hasselquist [=Fredrik Hasselquist, Iter Palaestinum (1757)] (Travels, p. 363), who described this serpent most accurately. I shall extract only a little. "Head slightly depressed on top, strongly depressed between the eyes [III, 129], strongly protruding at the sides and raised from the body. — Tail below the anus conical, short, tapering, ending at the tip in a slightly curved spine. — In Egypt everything that the pharmacopoeias require from the viper is taken from this: salt of viper, dried viper flesh, viper troches are all prepared from it, both for the use of the inhabitants and for export to Europe." — Niebuhr [=Carsten Niebuhr, Beschreibung von Arabien (1772)] in the Preface to the Description of Arabia, p. XL, mentions a certain serpent called Afa by the Arabs, about which the inhabitants of those regions tell many fables. Oedmann (Fasc. 4, Chapter 8, p. 78) takes this serpent for our أفعي [afʿī]; but the spelling does not agree, for Niebuhr writes the name Äfae as افاة [afāh]. Moreover, what the Arabs relate of the Afa, that it kills by its hiss alone, agrees better with the fables of the ancients about the basilisk. See Bochart below, Chapter IX.
notes.label: R2

notes.text: That these stories about vipers are fables is shown by Buffon's continuator, de La Cépède, vol. 2, Hist. Nat. des Serpens, p. 35.
notes.label: R3

notes.text: Albert Schultens inquired more precisely into the origin and various meanings of the verb فعي [faʿā] in his Notes on the Hamasa Anthology, appended to Erpenius's Grammar, pp. 420–421. From the Arab lexicographers he shows that فعي [faʿā] properly means he blew with puffed-out mouth, whence it is used of a woman in labour who, having long held her breath, at last, overcome by pain, bursts out with a gasping cry.
notes.label: R4

notes.text: This artful etymology seems unnecessary. The viper seems to have been given the name אפעה, افعي [afʿī] from hissing and from blowing with open, or rather puffed-out, mouth.
notes.label: R5
